meta.title: String stars, small black holes, and the supersymmetric index
meta.abstractHtml:
We discuss aspects of the black hole-string transition as the angular velocity approaches the supersymmetric index . In this limit, the high-temperature Atick-Witten effective description breaks down. For Heterotic string theory, a new high-temperature description emerges near the index in terms of a Higgsed supergravity with a magnetic field profile. The Hagedorn instability manifests in the theory as Ambjørn–Olesen W boson condensation, due to the background magnetic field. For type II, a tower of winding strings becomes light near the index, which opens up a new dimension in the T-dual picture. In both cases, a string star solution is found, similar to the Horowitz-Polchinski solution, but decouples at the index .
Considering charged solutions, the string star appears to interpolate between charged black holes and the free string phase. At the index, both the charged black hole and the charged string star phases decouple. This suggests a tension between a smooth black hole-string transition and the existence of a stringy BPS two-charge black hole.

children.title: Abstract
children.body:
We discuss aspects of the black hole-string transition as the angular velocity approaches the supersymmetric index . In this limit, the high-temperature Atick-Witten effective description breaks down. For Heterotic string theory, a new high-temperature description emerges near the index in terms of a Higgsed supergravity with a magnetic field profile. The Hagedorn instability manifests in the theory as Ambjørn–Olesen W boson condensation, due to the background magnetic field. For type II, a tower of winding strings becomes light near the index, which opens up a new dimension in the T-dual picture. In both cases, a string star solution is found, similar to the Horowitz-Polchinski solution, but decouples at the index .
Considering charged solutions, the string star appears to interpolate between charged black holes and the free string phase. At the index, both the charged black hole and the charged string star phases decouple. This suggests a tension between a smooth black hole-string transition and the existence of a stringy BPS two-charge black hole.

The high-energy spectrum of quantum gravity is dominated by black holes. In weakly coupled string theories, there is an intermediate high energy limit dominated by highly excited strings with a Hagedorn growth [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. It is an old question [6, 7, 8], whether these two thermodynamic phases are secretly one and the same. Namely, if a high-temperature black hole (say in the last stages of evaporation) transitions to a self-gravitating string state, or a ‘string star’. This is sometimes referred to as the black hole/ string transition. Since the two phases have no reliable overlapping region, attempts to argue for or against them have always been mostly qualitative.

gist.html: Black holes dominate at high energy, excited strings with Hagedorn growth in between; whether a shrinking black hole becomes a string star is an old, so far qualitative, question.

children.body: This work studies the fate of the black hole/ string transition at the (target space) -BPS supersymmetric index of either Heterotic or type II strings on . This index can be reached continuously from the thermal partition function, by turning on an angular velocity at . For a given set of charges , the exact index is known [9, 10] by a free string theory calculation. One may ask for the contribution of either the black hole or the string star to the index, by following them to the value . Since the index is independent of temperature and string coupling, agreement or disagreement between the two phases and the microscopic answer could shed light on the nature and validity of the string-black hole transition itself.

gist.html: The paper follows both phases to the $\tfrac12$-BPS index, $\beta\Omega = 2\pi i$, which is known exactly and independent of temperature and coupling.

children.title: The index as a twisted partition function
children.body: A supersymmetric theory has a conserved fermion number $(-1)^F$ and supercharges that pair every state of non-zero energy with a partner of opposite statistics. In the trace $\operatorname{Tr}\,e^{-\beta H}(-1)^F$ such pairs cancel, so only states annihilated by some supercharges, the BPS states, contribute, and the result does not change with $\beta$ or with any continuous coupling. For strings on $\mathbb R^d$ the relevant object is a $\tfrac12$-BPS index that counts states with given momentum and winding charges; it can be computed at zero string coupling and gives $S_\text{micro}=4\pi\sqrt{|Q_nQ_w|}$. The paper's observation is that this index is also a point in a continuous family: since rotating by $2\pi$ gives $(-1)^F=e^{2\pi iJ}$, inserting $e^{-\beta\Omega J}$ with $\beta\Omega=2\pi i$ into the thermal partition function produces exactly the index, so one can turn the angular velocity on gradually and watch each saddle of the thermal problem move towards $\nu=0$.

Unlike the black hole, it is not clear at all how to deform the string star saddle away from the thermal case. To understand why, let us recall what the string star saddle really is. We denote the radius of the thermal circle. Viewing the canonical partition function as a Euclidean string amplitude, a mode with a single winding along the thermal circle turns tachyonic for , accounting for the Hagedorn growth of string states. Upon reducing on the thermal circle, one obtains the Atick-Witten effective field theory (EFT) [5], which includes all the standard massless spectrum, together with a “thermal scalar”: a complex scalar with mass . The string star saddle, or the Horowitz-Polchinski solution [11, 12], is a normalizable solution for the thermal scalar coupled to Newtonian gravity.1 The Atick-Witten EFT is reliable as long as the thermal scalar mass is light, which happens slightly below the Hagedorn temperature . Perturbatively in , one can employ the Atick-Witten EFT to find slowly rotating string star solutions [16]. But as we turn on , the potential for the thermal scalar becomes string-sized, leading to an unreliable EFT. Thus, it appears hopeless to reliably deform the string star saddle to the index.

gist.html: The string star is the Horowitz–Polchinski solution of the Atick–Witten EFT, valid only for $R-R_H\ll1$; at $\Omega\sim O(1)$ the thermal scalar's potential is string-sized and the EFT fails.

children.title: The thermal circle, the winding tachyon and the Atick–Witten theory
children.body: A thermal partition function is a Euclidean path integral with time compactified on a circle of circumference $\beta=2\pi R$. For strings there is a new kind of state: a closed string wound once around this circle, with mass $m^2\sim R^2-R_H^2$ in string units. Above the Hagedorn temperature ($R

Surprisingly, although the Atick-Witten EFT breaks down, we find a novel EFT close to the supersymmetric point . In section 2, we begin with Heterotic string theory. At the index, the thermal circle admits a (periodic) supersymmetric boundary condition for the fermions. At the self-dual radius (in string units), the effective -dimensional theory is half-maximal gauged supergravity. Away from the self-dual point, the theory is higgsed back to the standard KK gauge group. This gauge enhancement is a well-known property of Heterotic string theory [30, 31].2 For temperatures close to the self-dual radius , the EFT is reliable. The winding mode takes place in the EFT as the W boson. Due to supersymmetry, the W boson is stable, which agrees with the absence of a Hagedorn instability due to supersymmetric cancellations. By going slightly away from , the Hagedorn instability is restored, and the theory should have a tachyon. In the EFT, this instability has an elegant explanation. Changing amounts to a magnetic field profile for the unbroken in the direction of the rotation plane. Since the W boson is charged, its mass is affected by the magnetic field. The result is known as the Ambjørn–Olesen phenomenon [32, 33, 34], in which the electroweak W boson condenses if the background magnetic field is high enough compared to the Higgs VEV. In our context, it explains how the winding mode (W boson) turns tachyonic away from the index (magnetic field) at high temperatures (small Higgs VEV).

gist.html: Heterotic strings have a new EFT near the index: at $R=1$ the gauge group is enhanced to $SU(2)_L\times U(1)_R$, the winding mode is its W boson, and the Hagedorn instability is Ambjørn–Olesen condensation in the magnetic field that $\nu$ creates.

children.body: In section 3, we look for string star solutions close to the index. In terms of the EFT, we work close to the critical magnetic field and look for a bubble of W boson condensation. We call those solutions ‘W stars’. Similar to the Horowitz-Polchinski solution, these solutions include a winding-mode profile as well as the gravitational (and magnetic) forces needed to support it. The solution shares many properties with the Horowitz-Polchinski solution, with a notable difference: the W star decouples as we tune back to the index . As we explain, this property is also shared by rotating black holes in this limit.

gist.html: Section 3 finds “W stars”, bubbles of W condensate analogous to Horowitz–Polchinski, which decouple as $\nu\to0$, as rotating black holes do.

children.body: Next, in section 4, we use the method put forward in [12] and consider charged solutions. Slightly away from the index, we find such charged W stars and study their properties. Similar to [12], our solutions appear to interpolate between the charged rotating black hole and the free string phase and approach the correct microscopic index . This is drastically different than the charged black hole saddle, where a naive continuation to the index gives a vanishing index. Exactly at the index, however, both the weakly curved charged black hole and the charged W star are unreliable and decouple from the spectrum. Thus, we argue that a smooth black hole/string transition contradicts the existence of a BPS ‘small black hole’ solution of the type recently suggested in [35, 36].

gist.html: Section 4 adds charges: charged W stars interpolate between charged black holes and free strings and approach the microscopic index, while exactly at the index both charged phases decouple, in tension with a BPS small black hole.

children.body: In section 5 we comment on the type II case. Close to the index, an arbitrary number of winding strings become light at the same time. Thus, the EFT in this case is the T-dual dimensional SUGRA [37]. We argue that string star solutions exist with properties similar to the Heterotic W star. In section 6 we consider Bosonic string theory, and explain a possible issue with the black hole/string transition when turning on large imaginary . We close with conclusions and future directions.

gist.html: Section 5 treats type II, where a tower of windings becomes light and the EFT is the T-dual $(d+1)$-dimensional supergravity; section 6 raises a bosonic-string puzzle at large imaginary $\beta\Omega$.

Can a hot black hole turn into a self-gravitating string? The supersymmetric index, reached by $\beta\Omega=2\pi i$, offers a quantitative test, and near it a new effective description replaces Atick–Witten.

brief.html: At high energies quantum gravity is black holes, but weakly coupled strings have an intermediate regime of highly excited strings with Hagedorn growth, and whether a black hole in the last stages of evaporation becomes a self-gravitating string state, a string star, has only been argued qualitatively because the two phases have no reliable overlap. The paper follows both phases to the $\tfrac12$-BPS index, reached from the thermal partition function by $\beta\Omega=2\pi i$; the index is known exactly and is independent of temperature and coupling, so agreement with the microscopic answer tests the transition itself. The string star is the Horowitz–Polchinski solution of the Atick–Witten effective theory for the thermal winding scalar, reliable only for $R-R_H\ll1$ and small $\Omega$; at $\Omega\sim O(1)$ the thermal scalar's potential is string-sized and the saddle cannot be followed. Yet a new effective theory exists near the index for heterotic strings: at the self-dual radius the theory is the half-maximal $SU(2)_L\times U(1)_R$ gauged supergravity, Higgsed away from $R=1$, the winding mode is its W boson, and turning on $\nu$ is a magnetic field that makes the W tachyonic, the Ambjørn–Olesen phenomenon. The paper then finds W stars, bubbles of W condensate that decouple as $\nu\to0$ like rotating black holes; adds charges, where charged W stars approach the microscopic index while both charged phases decouple at the index, in tension with a BPS small black hole; treats type II, where a tower of windings becomes light and the effective theory is the T-dual $(d+1)$-dimensional supergravity; and raises a puzzle for bosonic strings.

children.title: Gauge enhancement at the self-dual radius
children.body: A heterotic string on a circle of radius $R$ has two $U(1)$ gauge fields from the circle, the Kaluza–Klein vector and the $B$-field vector, or in a chiral basis $U(1)_L\times U(1)_R$, with the radius itself appearing as a massless scalar. The W boson is therefore the string with winding $\pm1$, which is exactly the thermal winding mode when the circle is the thermal one.

A self-gravitating normalizable condensate solution of the scalar was found by Horowitz and Polchinski [11]. By expanding in small , it was possible to consider only the leading Newtonian gravity cubic coupling, which led to a self-consistent background for spatial dimensions. This background was proposed [11, 12] as a stringy description of high-temperature black holes.

children.body: Susskind, and Horowitz and Polchinski, proposed that a black hole shrinking by Hawking evaporation becomes, when its horizon reaches the string scale, a single long excited string: at that point the black hole entropy $S\sim r_h^{D-2}/G_N$ and the string entropy $S\sim l_sE$ match, up to order-one factors, for $g_s^2S\sim1$. Horowitz and Polchinski later found the self-gravitating string state as a solution of the Atick–Witten theory: the light thermal scalar sources a Newtonian potential through a cubic coupling, and in $2

How would such a solution look like if we were to follow it with close to the index ? Compactifying spatial directions, the partition function (2.1) corresponds to a -dimensional Melvin background. Close enough to , the effective theory is the -dimensional reduction of the 9d SUGRA theory spelled in the previous section. Instead of a thermal scalar, a winding condensate corresponds to a normalizable saddle for the W boson. Below, we will show how to find such a solution in the theory.

gist.html: Near the index the analogue is a normalisable W boson saddle of the $d$-dimensional reduction of the $SU(2)$ SUGRA on the Melvin background.

children.body: At the index, the background is supersymmetric, the Lagrangian is entirely positive, and admits no normalizable saddles.13 Thus, at there are no “W stars” saddles. This is a striking difference with the Atick-Witten EFT. The application of this statement for the correspondence with black holes will be discussed below. For now, the lesson is that in order to find such saddles we must turn on , and shouldn’t treat it as a perturbative parameter. Such a saddle can be thought of as a meta-stable bubble of the W condensation phase. The existence of a high-temperature W boson tachyon for , established in the previous section, is a positive signal that such a bubble solution could be formed.

gist.html: At $\nu=0$ the Lagrangian is positive and has no normalisable saddles, so $\nu>0$ must be kept finite; the saddle is a metastable bubble of the W condensate phase.

children.body: Terminology The term “Horowitz-Polchinski solution" will describe the solution for the thermal-scalar Atick-Witten EFT [11] and its possible generalizations. “W star” will describe only W boson normalizable condensate solutions of the Heterotic EFT. To describe any normalizable string theory saddle of thermal winding strings, we will use the term “string stars” collectively. Thus, both the Horowitz-Polchinski solution and W stars are types of string stars, but not the other way around.

gist.html: Terminology: Horowitz–Polchinski solution (Atick–Witten EFT), W star ($SU(2)$ EFT), string star (any normalisable winding saddle).

children.body: Let us assume that in the controlled, slowly rotating, regime , the black hole and the string star saddles are continuously related as a function of the temperature. The unavoidable outcome appears to be that the discontinuity at should develop at an intermediate temperature. This is confusing, since we usually think about such discontinuities as resolved by non-perturbative effects (as in the Hawking-Page transition, for example). Since our entire discussion is at tree level, it seems inevitable that stringy effects resolve the discontinuity at sufficiently high temperatures. It is not clear to us if this tension contradicts the black hole/string transition itself (at least for the Bosonic string) or not.

gist.html: The transition was studied near the index, $\beta\Omega=2\pi i(1-\nu)$, where the answer depends on the string theory.

children.body: For Heterotic strings, we found that instead of the Atick-Witten theory, the effective description is a Higgsed SUGRA, in which the winding mode is the W boson. The Hagedorn instability is manifest (for ) via a version of the Ambjørn–Olesen phenomenon. The string star in this regime is a bubble of W boson condensate, with properties similar to the Horowitz-Polchinski solution. In the limit, the string star decouples from the spectrum, just like the weakly-curved black hole. For type II string theory, an arbitrary number of winding strings are light together for , leading to a new T-dual dimension. The effective -dimensional theory admits a somewhat complicated tachyonic mode for [37]. Nonetheless, a string star solution arguably exists in an appropriate low-energy limit, leading to similar results.

gist.html: Heterotic: Higgsed $SU(2)_L\times U(1)_R$ SUGRA, Ambjørn–Olesen instability, W star decoupling at $\nu=0$ like the black hole; type II: a T-dual dimension and a string star in a low-energy limit.

children.body: String star solutions with NS-NS charges can be found by generalizing the method put forward in [12], for both Heterotic and type II string theories. The same picture suggested in [12] seems to hold for , in which the string star interpolates between the free string and the black hole phase. Following the uncharged case, the charged string star decouples in the limit. This suggests that both the black hole and the string star phases decouple, leaving only a BPS string phase. However, this picture is in tension with the small black hole saddle suggested recently for the index [35, 36].

gist.html: Charged string stars interpolate between free strings and black holes for $0<\nu\ll1$ and decouple at $\nu=0$, leaving a BPS string phase, in tension with the proposed small black hole saddle.

children.body: For Heterotic strings, the transition to the BPS string phase appears to be smooth. Specifically, for large charges, the charged string star entropy approaches the microscopic BPS entropy. For type II, the transition could be smooth, but requires some crossover in the free string phase from a generic highly-excited string and a BPS string. It would be interesting to find a possible connection to the worldsheet index arguments of [12]. We leave these questions for future work.

gist.html: For heterotic the transition to BPS strings looks smooth; for type II it needs a Hagedorn-to-BPS crossover; a connection to the worldsheet index arguments of [12] is left open.

children.body: Using the new effective description for the winding mode near the index, several extensions of this work come to mind. First, we tuned the winding mass to satisfy for convenience, which allows us to consider only the ground state. It would be interesting to study the full solution at intermediate values of the temperatures . Similarly, the Wilson coefficients of the -dimensional theory can in principle be found for any through a worldsheet computation. This could help to gather evidence that the self-force of the winding mode remains attractive and supports the picture we suggested. Thirdly, one can consider several angular velocities at the same time, which will lead in the limit to an even-lower-dimensional theory. For example in we can turn on , which would result in a zero-dimensional theory for . It could be interesting to check that the effective force in this case is also attractive, and to study properties of the W star. It could also be interesting to turn on thermal Wilson lines for the Heterotic gauge fields and study how the solution changes as a result, especially close to new gauge-enhancement points.

gist.html: Extensions: intermediate temperatures $m^2\sim\nu$, Wilson coefficients from the worldsheet, several angular velocities (a zero-dimensional theory in $D=5$), and thermal Wilson lines near other enhancement points.

children.body: Finally, for Bosonic string theory, we spelled out an important qualitative difference between the black hole and the string star phases. Namely, the black hole has a first-order phase transition at , while the string star has none. Both type II and Heterotic avoid this issue: since both are Fermionic theories, , the phase transition could occur at , not , and second, both the black hole and, due to supersymmetry, the string star decouple at . A different version of this issue arises for fermionic but non-supersymmetric string theories. While the black hole free energy still diverges at , we no longer expect the string star to diverge (the partition function still admits a Hagedorn growth).

gist.html: Bosonic strings have a first-order black hole transition at $\omega=\pi$ with no string-star counterpart; fermionic theories push it to $\omega=2\pi$ where supersymmetric theories decouple, and non-supersymmetric fermionic theories pose a different version of the issue.

Summary: heterotic winding mode as W boson, Hagedorn instability as Ambjørn–Olesen, W stars that decouple at the index like black holes; type II needs a T-dual dimension; charged string stars approach the microscopic index but decouple, in tension with BPS small black holes; extensions and the bosonic puzzle.

brief.html: Near the index the analysis depends on the string theory: heterotic strings are described by a Higgsed $SU(2)_L imes U(1)_R$ supergravity whose W boson is the winding mode, with the Hagedorn instability as Ambjørn–Olesen condensation and a string star that decouples at $ u=0$ like the black hole; type II strings need a T-dual dimension and still admit a string star in a low-energy limit. Charged string stars interpolate between free strings and black holes for $0< u\ll1$ and decouple at $ u=0$, leaving a BPS string phase, in tension with the proposed small black hole; the heterotic transition looks smooth, the type II one needs a Hagedorn-to-BPS crossover. Extensions include intermediate temperatures, worldsheet Wilson coefficients, several angular velocities and thermal Wilson lines; for bosonic strings the black hole has a first-order transition at $\omega=\pi$ that the string star does not, an issue that fermionic theories postpone to $\omega=2\pi$.

gist.html:
• Context Does a hot black hole in string theory turn, as it shrinks, into a self-gravitating ball of excited string (a “string star”)? The two phases have no overlapping regime of validity, so the black hole/string transition has only ever been argued qualitatively. The supersymmetric index is a sharper test: it is reached from the thermal partition function by an imaginary angular velocity $\beta\Omega = 2\pi i$, it is known exactly from free strings, and it does not depend on the temperature or the coupling, so each phase can be followed to it and compared.
  • Result Near the index the usual near-Hagedorn (Atick–Witten) description fails, but for heterotic strings a new one takes over: a Higgsed $SU(2)_L\times U(1)_R$ supergravity in which the thermal winding mode is the W boson, the angular velocity is a magnetic field, and the Hagedorn instability is Ambjørn–Olesen W condensation. The string star becomes a “W star”, a bubble of W condensate much like the Horowitz–Polchinski solution; for type II strings a whole tower of windings becomes light and the effective theory is the T-dual $(d+1)$-dimensional supergravity, with a similar string star. In both cases the string star decouples exactly at the index, as the weakly curved black hole does. With charges, the W star interpolates between charged black holes and free strings and approaches the microscopic index $2\pi\sqrt{Q_R^2-Q_L^2}$.
  • Why it matters Exactly at the index both the charged black hole and the charged string star decouple, leaving only a BPS string phase. A smooth black hole/string transition is therefore in tension with a BPS “small black hole” saddle for the index, as recently proposed. Along the way the paper writes the 9d $SU(2)_L\times U(1)_R$ gauged supergravity to all orders in the fields at two derivatives, and exhibits a first-order discontinuity that the bosonic string's black holes have and its string stars do not.

student.html:
• Context String theory has two kinds of very energetic objects: black holes, and long, highly excited strings. An old conjecture says a black hole that heats up as it evaporates turns smoothly into a ball of string held together by its own gravity. Nobody has been able to check this, because no calculation is reliable in between. This paper uses a trick: a quantity called the supersymmetric index, which counts certain states exactly and cannot depend on the temperature, so one can ask what each of the two phases contributes to it.
  • Result Approaching the index, the string that winds around the thermal circle, which normally behaves like a scalar particle, becomes a charged vector particle: the W boson of a gauge theory that lives inside heterotic string theory. The rotation that brings one to the index acts on it like a magnetic field, and the familiar fact that a strong enough magnetic field makes W bosons condense turns out to be the string's Hagedorn instability in disguise. The author finds the corresponding “string star” (a W star), shows that it disappears exactly at the index, and shows that black holes disappear there too. With electric charges added, the string star's entropy approaches the exact microscopic count.
  • Why it matters If both the black hole and the string star vanish at the index, only free BPS strings remain; this argues against a recently proposed black hole saddle for the index, and sharpens what a smooth black hole/string transition would have to look like.

brief.html:
At high energies the spectrum of quantum gravity is black holes, but a weakly coupled string theory has an intermediate regime, $1\ll l_sE\ll g_s^{-2}$, of highly excited strings with Hagedorn growth $S\sim 2\pi R_HE$, and it is an old question whether a black hole in the last stages of evaporation turns into a self-gravitating string state, a “string star”. The paper follows both phases to the $ frac12$-BPS supersymmetric index of heterotic or type II strings on $\mathbb R^d$, reached from the thermal partition function by an imaginary angular velocity $ eta\Omega = 2\pi i$; since the index is known exactly from free strings and is independent of temperature and coupling, agreement or disagreement is a quantitative statement about the transition. The difficulty is that the string star, the Horowitz–Polchinski solution of the Atick–Witten effective theory for the thermal winding scalar, cannot be deformed to the index: away from the thermal point the winding spectrum acquires string-scale gaps $\Delta m^2\sim|1- u|$ and the effective theory stops making sense.

For heterotic strings a new effective theory appears near the index. The twisted partition function is a Euclidean magnetic Melvin background with a graviphoton profile that encodes the angular velocity, and following the thermal winding mode to $ u=0$ on the worldsheet one finds that its mass is $(R-1/R)^2$, non-negative for every temperature, and that it is no longer a scalar but a massive complex vector; it becomes massless at the self-dual radius $R=1$, where the heterotic gauge group is enhanced from $U(1)_L imes U(1)_R$ to $SU(2)_L imes U(1)_R$. The low-energy theory near $R=1$ is therefore the half-maximal $SU(2)_L imes U(1)_R$ gauged supergravity, which the paper writes to all orders in the fields at two derivatives; the radius is the vacuum value of an adjoint Higgs, and in unitary gauge the winding mode is the W boson, with mass $m_W^2 = (R-1/R)^2$. Turning on $ u$ is a magnetic field for the unbroken gauge group: the W boson spectrum organises into Landau levels that reproduce the worldsheet masses, the magnetic dipole (Zeeman) coupling lowers the longitudinal polarisation, and the ground state turns tachyonic for $R

A string star near the index is a bubble of W condensate, a “W star”. At $ u=0$ the Lagrangian is positive and admits no normalisable saddle, so $ u$ must be kept finite; expanding the $SU(2)$ action near the Hagedorn point gives a cubic theory in which the W boson sources the Newtonian potential and the Kaluza–Klein vector, and integrating those out yields gravitational attraction between $|W|^2$ densities and an Ampère force between winding currents. When the winding ground state is much lighter than the Landau gap, $m^2\ll u\ll1$, only its $(d-2)$-dimensional momentum modes matter, and the theory reduces to a single scalar with a long-range kernel that is marginal and logarithmically regulated by the vortex size $|z|^2\sim1/ u$; a variational solution exists for $2 The W star has action $I\sim m^{6-d}/( u\log( u/m^2))$ and obeys $S_ u = 2\pi l_sE$, a Hagedorn relation that survives next to an index that has no Hagedorn temperature; it transitions to free strings when $I\sim1$, and as $ u o0$ at fixed temperature it does not dissolve but decouples with diverging action and amplitude. Rotating (Myers–Perry) black holes behave the same way: at fixed temperature the $ u o0$ limit sends the horizon radius, mass and spin to infinity for $D>4$ (the mass stays finite in $D=4$), and extrapolating both saddles to intermediate temperatures gives the same $ u$ divergence of mass, entropy and size for $D>4$, so the two phases decouple together.

For a non-trivial index one needs charges. An $O(2,2;\mathbb R)$ transformation of the asymptotic $S^1_R imes S^1_r$ geometry turns any neutral saddle into one carrying momentum and winding on $S^1_r$; the paper generalises the map of Chen, Maldacena and Witten to arbitrary thermal momentum $n$ and twist $ u$, and it is $\alpha'$-exact. Applied to a weakly curved black hole it reproduces the two-charge black hole, and at small $ u$ two limits exist: a slightly transformed one that decouples like the neutral hole, and a Sen-like one with large boost $\upbeta$ that naively reaches the BPS bound with non-zero area but vanishing index, where the supergravity solution is singular and only a weakly curved regime $T\gg T_* = 1/(G_N|Q| u^{D-4})$ is reliable. The charged W star has $S_ u = \pi(R_H-n/R_H)\sqrt{M^2-Q_R^2}+\pi(R_H+n/R_H)\sqrt{M^2-Q_L^2}$, which near the index reduces to $2\pi\sqrt{M^2-Q_L^2}$ and approaches the microscopic $S_ ext{micro} = 2\pi\sqrt{Q_R^2-Q_L^2}$; but its reliable temperature window, between the transition to black holes and the transition to free strings, moves to infinity as $ u o0$, so it too decouples. Its size at the free-string transition, $L^2\sim\sqrt{Q_nQ_w}$, is that of a generic BPS string, which suggests a smooth transition to a BPS string phase at the index.

For type II strings the winding ground state has mass $m^2 = w^2R^2-2 u w$, which vanishes at $R=0$ rather than at the self-dual radius, so near the index arbitrarily many winding sectors are light at once. No $d$-dimensional effective theory can hold that many fields, but in the T-dual picture the windings are momentum modes on a large circle and the effective theory is the $(d+1)$-dimensional type II supergravity on the T-dual Melvin background, whose tachyonic modes were identified by David, Gutperle, Headrick and Minwalla; in the $m^2\ll u$ limit a single mode condenses and a string star with the same properties as the W star is expected. The charged type II string star has $S_ u = \pi\sqrt{2 u}(\sqrt{M^2-Q_R^2}+\sqrt{M^2-Q_L^2})$, which seems to give a vanishing index at $ u=0$; the resolution is that the limits $ u o0$ and $M o\infty$ do not commute, as the free-string partition function shows, and a generic string crosses over from Hagedorn to BPS behaviour for $M\ll1/ u$.

For the bosonic string, which has no index, the string star is continuous under $\omega\mapsto\omega+2\pi$ while the dominant black hole action has a derivative discontinuity at $\omega=\pi$; if the two phases are continuously connected, this discontinuity must be resolved at intermediate temperatures by stringy effects, a tension the paper leaves open. The discussion summarises the picture: near the index the heterotic winding mode is a W boson and the string star a W boson condensate, type II needs a new T-dual dimension, both phases decouple at the index leaving a BPS string phase, in tension with a BPS small black hole saddle; extensions include intermediate temperatures $m^2\sim u$, several angular velocities, and thermal Wilson lines.

questions.q: Why is the supersymmetric index a good place to test the black hole/string transition?
questions.a: Because it is known exactly and cannot depend on the temperature or the coupling. The thermal partition function connects continuously to the index through the imaginary angular velocity $\beta\Omega=2\pi i$, so each saddle, black hole or string star, can be followed to $\nu=0$ and its contribution compared with the free-string count. Any mismatch is then a sharp statement, whereas in the thermal case the two phases never overlap.

questions.q: Why can't the Horowitz–Polchinski solution simply be followed to the index?
questions.a:
The twisted boundary conditions shift the oscillator frequencies of the rotation-plane fields by $
u$, so away from the thermal point the winding spectrum acquires gaps $\Delta m^2\sim|1-
u|$ in string units: for $
u\sim O(1)$ the thermal scalar's potential is string-sized and there is no light field to write an effective theory for. Only near $
u=0$ does the spectrum become dense again, with a different light field.

questions.q: Why is the winding mode a vector at the index and a scalar at the thermal point?
questions.a: At $\nu=0$ the right-moving level of the ground state is $\tilde N=\tfrac12$, a standard NS excitation $\psi^\mu_{-1/2}$, and it can be made with any of the worldsheet fermions $\psi^0,\dots,\psi^8$; the nine states form a 9d massive vector. At the thermal point the GSO projection allows $\tilde N=0$ instead, a single state, the scalar. The level flows between the two as in (2.11).

questions.q: What is new about the $SU(2)_L	imes U(1)_R$ supergravity action?
questions.a: The gauge enhancement itself is classic, and the theory had been written to cubic order in the fields; the paper fixes it to all orders in the fields at two derivatives, using the half-maximal gauged supergravity of appendix A, and checks that the W mass reproduces the worldsheet exactly. Unlike the Atick–Witten theory it is not an expansion in small amplitudes.

questions.a:
Transverse polarisations see the magnetic field as a scalar would: their spectrum is gapped Landau levels, all non-negative. The in-plane polarisations $w_\pm$ carry spin $\pm1$ along the field and get the magnetic dipole (Zeeman) shift $\pm2
u(1+R^{-2})$; $w_-$ is lowered, and its $k=	ilde k=0$ level reaches $m^2=(R-1/R)^2-2
u/R^2$, which is negative for $R<R_H(

questions.q: Why are there no W star solutions exactly at the index?
questions.a: At $\nu=0$ the background is supersymmetric and the Lagrangian is a sum of non-negative terms. Rescaling any putative localised saddle, $\phi(x)\to\phi(\lambda x)$, lowers a positive two-derivative action in $d>2$, so no normalisable extremum exists (footnote 13). The W star needs the Zeeman term, i.e. $\nu>0$, to make a condensate energetically favourable; it is a metastable bubble, not a perturbation of the index background.

The Newtonian kernel integrated over two vortices then falls off as $1/r^{d}$ in $d-2$ dimensions, which is marginal: the self-energy diverges logarithmically and is cut off by the vortex size $1/

questions.q: In what sense do the black hole and the W star agree near the index?
questions.a:
Neither can be trusted at the other's temperature, so both are extrapolated to the string scale $R\sim l_s$. For $D>4$ both then have mass, entropy and size that diverge as $
u	o0$; the powers differ ($
u^{4-D}$ versus $
u^{-1/2}$ for the mass, $1/
u$ versus $1/\sqrt
u$ for the size), so the agreement is in the qualitative fact that both decouple, not in the exponents. $D=4$ is less clear because the black hole mass stays finite.

questions.q: What is the Sen limit, and why is the small black hole controversial?
questions.a: Boosting a weakly curved neutral black hole with $\upbeta\to\infty$ while its mass goes to zero reaches the BPS bound $M=|Q_R|$ with $S=\pi\tilde R\sqrt{Q_R^2-Q_L^2}$: the right charge dependence, but the limit passes through string-scale seed temperatures where supergravity fails, and in GR the horizon area vanishes. Some argue $\alpha'$ corrections give it a finite area matching $S_\text{micro}$, others that it stays singular; the paper's alternative is a transition to a charged string star.

questions.q: Does the charged W star reproduce the microscopic index?
questions.a: Approximately. With the W star's Hagedorn equation of state the solution-generating map gives, near the heterotic index, $S_\nu=2\pi\sqrt{M^2-Q_L^2}$, and in the large-boost limit it saturates the BPS bound with $S_\text{index}\approx2\pi\sqrt{Q_R^2-Q_L^2}=S_\text{micro}$, approached as $e^{-2\upbeta}$. But no W star saturates the bound exactly, and the window of temperatures in which it is reliable disappears as $\nu\to0$.

questions.q: What exactly is the tension with BPS small black holes?
questions.a: If the black hole/string transition is smooth, the charged black hole continues into the charged W star, and the paper finds that both decouple at the index, the W star ending as a BPS string phase of the right size $L^2\sim\sqrt{Q_nQ_w}$. Then nothing black-hole-like contributes at $\nu=0$, contrary to the recently proposed BPS small black hole saddle. The alternative is that the black hole and the W star are not connected at all.

questions.q: Why is type II so different from heterotic near the index?
questions.a: For type II the winding ground state has $m^2=R^2-2\nu$, the classical winding energy with no quantum shift, so it is light only at $R\ll1$ and then every winding number up to $w\sim1/\sqrt\nu$ is light at once. No $d$-dimensional theory can hold that many fields; the T-dual circle is large and the right description is supergravity in one more dimension. Heterotic strings instead have a single light winding sector, at the self-dual radius, with a finite gauge theory.

questions.q: Why does the type II index seem to vanish, and how is that resolved?
questions.a:
The charged entropy carries a factor $\sqrt{2
u}$, because a generic type II string at fixed $
u$ excites both chiralities and is far from BPS. The free-string partition function shows the limits do not commute: at fixed $
u$ it grows as $e^{
u/B}$, at $
u=0$ as $e^{2/B}$. For masses $M\ll1/
u$ a generic state is approximately BPS, so the free-string phase that the string star transitions into crosses over to the BPS entropy at lower mass.

The bosonic partition function is periodic in $\omega=-i\beta\Omega$ with period $2\pi$, and the string star respects this continuously. The black hole phase respects it only after summing branches, which leaves a first-order (derivative) discontinuity at $\omega=\pi$. If the two phases are continuously connected in temperature, the discontinuity has to appear somewhere in between and be resolved by tree-level stringy effects, which is unusual for a first-order transition.

questions.q: What is the Hagedorn growth of states, and why does it matter here?
questions.a: The number of string states of energy $E$ grows like $e^{2\pi R_HE}$, exponentially in the energy rather than in a power, so the canonical partition function diverges above the Hagedorn temperature $1/(2\pi R_H)$. A black hole's entropy grows differently ($S\sim E^{(D-2)/(D-3)}$), so the question of which phase dominates, and whether one turns into the other, is a question about these two growth laws meeting at the string scale.

questions.q: In one sentence, what is a string star, and how is it unlike a black hole?
questions.a: A string star is a ball of thermally wound strings bound by the gravity (and here also the magnetic force) they source, described by an effective field theory of the light winding mode; it has no horizon, its size is set by the winding mass rather than by $G_NM$, and it exists only in a narrow window of temperatures near the Hagedorn point.
